en: When the sun heats the ocean, liquid water turns into invisible water vapor and rises into the cooler air to form clouds.
Magma cools and solidifies into hard igneous rocks like granite when it erupts from a volcano and loses its intense heat to the surrounding air.
Earthworms and bacteria break down dead leaves into dark, nutrient-rich humus, which improves the soil's ability to hold water for plant roots.
The Sun's massive gravitational pull constantly pulls planets toward it, keeping them in curved elliptical orbits instead of flying off into deep space.
As the Moon orbits Earth, the Sun illuminates different portions of its surface, causing the visible shape of the Moon to change through its phases.
During the day, land heats up faster than the ocean, causing warm air over the beach to rise and cool ocean air to rush inland.
When tectonic plates suddenly slip past each other along a fault line, they release stored energy as seismic waves that shake the ground.
A massive star collapses under its own gravity when it runs out of fuel, triggering a giant explosion called a supernova that scatters elements.
Greenhouse gases like carbon dioxide trap heat radiating from Earth's surface, warming the lower atmosphere and maintaining a habitable global climate.
Intense heat and extreme pressure deep underground bake and squeeze existing rocks, transforming limestone into marble without completely melting the original material.
Rainwater soaking into the ground filters through porous soil and rock layers, eventually collecting in underground aquifers that store fresh water for wells.
Warm ocean water evaporates and rises, releasing latent heat that powers the spinning storm system of a typhoon and fuels its destructive winds.
